topic: formal verification; model checking; hybrid systems; industrial safety
status: bounded synthesis of six citation-follow-up papers from one 2015 proceedings volume; falsifiable evaluation hypothesis, not a pooled speedup estimate
claim: Verification evidence in this follow-up shows concrete engineering value, but the outcome depends on model structure and the property being proved. The railway case detects injected application-data errors and reports lower formula-development effort; a PVS case study exposes an initialization failure and a missing assumption; selected hybrid models see very large decomposition-time reductions while another example is unchanged. These results support testing for structure- and obligation-specific benefit, not a general claim that formal methods are faster or prevent failures at a known rate.
positive_evidence: Hybrid-system decomposition falls from 13h22m to 0.05s on complete K5 and 1h46m to 0.06s on Spidercam after graph relaxation, while cruise-controller runtime remains 0.060s.
The railway case models one station with 14 routes, 7 points and 7 track circuits; 132 invariants and 7 CTL properties identify injected data errors.

The aircraft cut-set example takes 13 minutes with systematic generation versus 65 minutes for a naive strategy, with the same reported set; two PVS case studies expose an initialization failure and an omitted implementation assumption.
counterevidence: The evidence comes from separate papers and incompatible endpoints: proof runtime, specification authoring effort, injected-error detection, and requirement/assumption discovery cannot be pooled.
The hybrid relaxation is conservative and its gains vary by model; the cruise-controller example shows no runtime improvement, and loose relaxation can trigger costly reconstruction.

The railway and cut-set results are single-model case studies; the latter assumes analyst-specified fault modes, and the proceedings do not provide controlled evidence of deployment-level defect reduction.

falsifiable_test: On an independently maintained, preregistered suite of industrial models, stratify by graph density, timing granularity, model size, and property family. Compare each abstraction/relaxation against the same baseline, hardware, and tool version. Measure proved-property coverage, abstraction soundness, runtime, memory, human modeling effort, injected-defect detection, and fallback rate. The hypothesis weakens if performance and coverage gains are stable across these strata and independent model families.
limitations: All six follow-ups come from one proceedings volume selected from a 2015 workshop and are not independent random sample observations. Most evidence is bounded to named examples and papers, not deployment evaluations; numerical outcomes use distinct setups and should not be meta-analyzed.
